title: Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Test Review and Other Measures) Bill 2009

divisions.question: The majority voted against [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2009-09-16.8.2) introduced by Liberal Senator [Concetta Fierravanti-Wells](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/nsw/concetta_fierravanti-wells), which means they failed. Learn more about the amendments in [Senator Fierravanti-Wells's explanation](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2009-09-16.8.2).

Kim Carr by leave—I move government amendments Nos (1), (2) and (3) on sheet Bm241 revised: (1) Clause 2, page 2 (at the end of the table), add: | 3. Schedule 2 | The day this Act receives the Royal Assent. | (2) Schedule 1, heading, page 3 (line 1), at the end of the heading, add “ **relating to citizenship test review etc.** ”. (3) Page 5 (after line 27), at the end of the bill, add: Schedule 2—Amendments relating to special residence requirement _Australian Citizenship Act 2007_ 1 Paragraph 21(2)(c) Omit “residence requirement (see section 22)”, substitute “general residence requirement (see section 22) or the special residence requirement (see section 22A or 22B)”. 2 Paragraph 21(3)(c) Omit “residence requirement (see section 22)”, substitute “general residence requirement (see section 22) or the special residence requirement (see section 22A or 22B)”. 3 Paragraph 21(4)(d) Omit “residence requirement (see section 22)”, substitute “general residence requirement (see section 22) or the special residence requirement (see section 22A or 22B)”. 4 Subsection 22(1) Omit “ **_residence requirement_** ”, substitute “ **_general residence requirement_** ”. Note: The heading to section 22 is replaced by the heading “ **General residence requirement** ”. 5 After section 22 Insert: 22A Special residence requirement—persons engaging in activities that are of benefit to Australia (1) Subject to this section, for the purposes of section 21 a person (the **_applicant_** ) satisfies the **_special residence requirement_** if: (a) the following apply: (i) the applicant is seeking to engage in an activity specified under subsection 22C(1); (ii) the applicant’s engagement in that activity would be of benefit to Australia; (iii) the applicant needs to be an Australian citizen in order to engage in that activity; (iv) in order for the applicant to engage in that activity, there is insufficient time for the applicant to satisfy the general residence requirement (see section 22); and (b

That this bill be now read a second time. That all words after “That” be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:“the House defers consideration of the bill until the following have occurred: That all words after “That” be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:“the House defers consideration of the bill until the following have occurred: That the words proposed to be omitted ( **Dr Stone’s** amendment) stand part of the question.

The majority voted against [amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2009-09-17.31.1) introduced by Liberal MP [Sharman Stone](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/murray/sharman_stone), which means they were unsuccessful. Read more about the amendments and MP Stone's [explanation for them](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2009-09-17.31.1).

The majority voted in favour of the bill. In parliamentary jargon, they agreed to the bill in detail. Now they just need to vote on whether they agree with the final wording of the bill (known as reading the bill for a [third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html)). ### What does the bill do? This bill was introduced to, for example: * make it easier for persons who have a physical or mental incapacity as a result of suffering torture or trauma before coming to Australia to be eligible to apply for citizenship; * allow prospective applicants for citizenship by conferral to sit the citizenship test at the same time as making the application; and * tighten the eligibility provisions for persons under 18 years of age by requiring that they be permanent residents; and * introduce a reduced period of residency for Australian citizenship for people in special circumstances. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd0910/10bd020).

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to introduce bills for a National Security Legislation Monitor, amendments to the Australian Citizenship Act 2007, and amendments to the Migration Act 1958. The motions were agreed to and the bills read a first time.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: The speaker introduced three bills: the National Security Legislation Monitor Bill 2009 to establish an independent reviewer of counter‑terrorism and national security laws; the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Test Review and Other Measures) Bill 2009 to implement 27 recommendations from the Citizenship Test Review Committee, including exemptions for torture and trauma survivors and a streamlined application process; and the Migration Amendment (Immigration Detention Reform) Bill 2009 to legislate seven key detention values, including that children will not be held in immigration detention centres.

speeches.speaker: Anne McEwen
speeches.brief: The Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee’s report on the Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Test Review and Other Measures) Bill 2009 was presented and ordered to be printed.

speeches.speaker: Concetta Fierravanti-Wells
speeches.brief: Senator Fierravanti-Wells (Coalition) supported streamlining citizenship applications and requiring under-18s to be permanent residents, but opposed removing mandatory questions on rights and responsibilities, retaining 'permanent' in the incapacity exemption, and rejected the proposed residency waivers for athletes. The Greens senator supported the bill but sought amendments to broaden the torture/trauma exemption to include harm suffered in Australia and to make the child's best interests the primary consideration for ministerial discretion.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Hanson-Young
speeches.brief: Minister Chris Evans announced government amendments creating a special residence requirement for citizenship covering people needing citizenship for activities of benefit to Australia and workers requiring regular overseas travel, with specified residency periods of two years’ permanent residency/six months in Australia or four years’ lawful residence/16 months in Australia. Greens, coalition and crossbench senators raised concerns about the torture/trauma exemption excluding victims trafficked in Australia, the permanent-residency requirement for minors, and the late introduction of the amendments.

speeches.speaker: Chris Evans
speeches.brief: The senator criticised the government for fast-tracking athlete citizenship and argued the citizenship test should not be weakened, citing a 97% pass rate. The senator supported a Greens amendment to replace "permanent" with "permanent or enduring" incapacity for citizenship test exemptions, and opposed a Greens amendment on minors' citizenship eligibility.

speeches.speaker: Concetta Fierravanti-Wells
speeches.brief: The opposition moved an amendment to create two limited ministerial discretions for granting citizenship in exceptional circumstances and for offshore workers, requiring non-delegable decisions and annual publication of recipients, arguing the government's rushed amendments were designed to fast-track citizenship for athletes like Russian ice skater Ms Borodulina and lacked proper scrutiny.
